title: Blood, nectar and fruit
teaches: Why vampire bats feed hungry roost-mates, how bats live on blood, nectar, fruit, fish and meat, and what nectar and fruit bats do for plants
summary: **Most bats eat insects, but not all.** Others live on nectar, fruit, fish, frogs, birds or, in three American species, blood.
**A vampire bat is always close to starving.** It needs a large meal of blood every night and dies after about 60 hours without one.
**Vampires find blood by heat and keep it flowing with spit.** Pit organs on the nose sense warm skin, and an anticoagulant in the saliva stops clotting while the bat laps.
**Vampires feed hungry roost-mates by bringing up blood.** Gerald Wilkinson saw it in Costa Rica and found that donors gave to kin and to bats they roosted with and that had fed them.
**A gift costs the donor fewer hours than it gives.** A full bat loses weight fast and a hungry one slowly, so the same few grams move the hungry bat much further from death.
**Sharing that remembers who gave is safe from cheats.** A bat that never gives is soon refused, while a rule of feeding everyone lets it take for free.

**Long-nosed bats carry agave pollen tens of kilometres in a night.** That is why wild agaves open their flowers in the dark, and why most commercial tequila agave, grown from clones, no longer needs them.
**Fruit bats drop seeds in flight.** Birds mostly drop seeds where they perch, so bats are the ones that seed the middle of a cleared patch and start the forest growing back.

blocks.text: Hacienda La Pacífica was a cattle ranch near Cañas, in the dry northwest of Costa Rica, in the province of Guanacaste. In the late 1970s and early 1980s Gerald Wilkinson, a graduate student from the University of California at San Diego, spent his nights there with the ranch's vampire bats. They roosted in groups in hollow trees around the pastures. He caught them, marked each so he could tell it from the rest, weighed them, and then watched the roosts in the hours before dawn as the bats came home from feeding on the cattle.

Many came home heavy. A few came home light, having found no animal to bite or been driven off one. And sometimes Wilkinson saw a light bat lick at the lips of a heavy one, and the heavy one bring up blood from its stomach into the other's mouth. He saw it 110 times. Seventy-seven of those were mothers feeding their own young. The other 33 were between bats that were not mother and child, and some of those bats were not related at all.

A vampire bat has no fat to speak of, and blood is the only food it can digest. Every meal it gives away is food it may need itself tomorrow. So why give? And if a bat is going to give, to whom? Wilkinson's answer, published in *Nature* in 1984, is the centre of this lesson. Hold the question while the lesson first explains what living on blood involves, since the answer turns on it.

Three species of bat drink blood, and all live in the Americas, from Mexico to Argentina. The **common vampire bat**, *Desmodus rotundus*, weighs about as much as a large mouse, 25 to 40 grams, and feeds mainly on mammals: cattle, horses and pigs since Europeans brought them, tapirs and deer before. The other two, the white-winged and hairy-legged vampires, mostly feed on birds. No bat in the Old World drinks blood.

A common vampire usually lands on the ground beside a sleeping animal and walks, hops or runs to it on its wings and thumbs, as few other bats can. It finds a place where blood runs close under the skin with heat sensors in three small pits around its nose. In 2011 Elena Gracheva, David Julius and colleagues found what makes them work: the nerve cells serving the pits use a shortened version of the protein, called TRPV1, that in our own skin makes us feel a burn at about 43 °C. The vampire's version switches on at about 30 °C, so the warmth of skin several centimetres away is enough to set it off.[^trpv1]

With its upper incisors, sharp as razors, it shaves away a little hair and cuts a shallow wound a few millimetres across. It does not suck. It laps, its tongue running in and out of the wound for twenty minutes or more, while its saliva keeps the blood flowing. The saliva carries an **anticoagulant**, a substance that stops blood clotting; one of them, a protein, was named **draculin** when it was described in the 1990s.[^draculin] A meal can weigh half the bat's own weight or more. Within minutes of starting to feed the bat begins passing the meal's water as urine, so that it can still take off.

Blood is mostly water and protein, with very little fat or sugar, so a vampire cannot store much. Wilkinson's weighings showed a bat losing weight steadily after a meal and dying about 60 hours later if it did not feed again: two missed nights in a row are usually fatal. On any night about one adult in fourteen failed to feed, and about one young bat in three.

blocks.caption: How the weight of a vampire bat falls after a full meal, and what a gift of 5 grams of blood does to the donor and to a hungry bat. An illustrative curve with the shape Wilkinson measured; the bat dies about 60 hours after its last meal.

blocks.text: The shape of that curve holds Wilkinson's first clue. A bat that has just fed is losing weight quickly, mostly water. Take a few grams of blood from it and it is set back only a few hours. A bat nearing starvation is losing weight slowly, so the same few grams put it most of a day further from death. A gift costs the giver much less time than it gives the receiver. That makes giving cheap, but it does not explain whom a bat should give to.

Biologists had two explanations for an animal helping another at a cost to itself. One is **kinship**: a relative shares many of your genes, so feeding a sister or a daughter helps copies of your genes survive. The other is **reciprocity**: help others and be helped in turn, which can work between unrelated animals as long as each remembers who helped and who refused. Reciprocity has a known weakness. A cheat that takes help but never gives saves its own food, and if nobody notices, cheats do better than givers and spread.

Wilkinson could test both because he knew, from years of records, which bats roosted together and, from their blood, roughly how related they were. Gifts went to relatives more often than chance, and also to bats that spent a lot of time in the same roost, whether related or not. Then he kept a small group of bats in captivity, some of them unrelated and taken from two different roosts. Each night he kept one bat from feeding and watched who fed it. The bats fed roost-mates they knew, and a bat was more likely to be fed by one it had itself fed before.

blocks.caption: A roost of thirty common vampires, six families of four adult females and a young bat, through a year of nights. Each bat feeds or fails at Wilkinson's rates; a bat dies 60 hours after its last meal. Choose the rule for sharing and add bats that cheat. A model, with gifts sized by the curve above.
blocks.task: Guess, then find the rule under which cheats lose

blocks.text: Without sharing, the arithmetic is grim: a bat that fails one night in fourteen will, sooner or later in a year, fail two nights running, and most would be dead within the year. Wilkinson worked this out from his rates: without sharing, about 82% of adults would die each year, while in the wild he found about a quarter dying. The model does better still, because no bat in it dies of anything but hunger. Sharing with family keeps most bats alive but carries cheats along with their families. Sharing with everyone lets cheats take and never pay. Only paying back starves them, because a cheat soon has no one who owes it a meal.

Gerald Carter, working with Wilkinson from about 2010, followed this further with captive colonies. Who had fed a bat before predicted who would feed it better than relatedness did. Bats that fed many partners were better off when one partner was taken away. And in 2020 Carter and colleagues showed how strangers become partners: two unfamiliar bats put together begin by grooming each other, and only after the grooming has built up does one first bring up blood for the other.[^carter]

Vampires are three species out of about 1,480. Roughly seven bat species in ten eat insects and other small animals with jointed legs, like every bat over Green Lake. The rest have found other food, and their faces show it. Nectar bats have long snouts and long tongues tipped with a brush of fine projections that sweep up nectar. Fruit bats have short, broad faces and strong jaws for crushing pulp. Insect-eaters have rows of small pointed teeth for cracking beetles and moths, and often large ears for hearing faint echoes.

A few eat larger animals. The greater bulldog bat of tropical America, *Noctilio leporinus*, hunts fish: it listens for the ripple where a fish's fin breaks the surface, then trails its long legs through the water and gaffs the fish with hooked claws. The fish-eating myotis, *Myotis vivesi*, lives on desert islands in the Gulf of California and flies out over the sea at night to snatch small fish and crustaceans from the waves. The fringe-lipped bat of Panama finds frogs by listening to their mating calls, which Merlin Tuttle and Michael Ryan showed in 1981 by playing recorded calls from speakers that the bats flew down to.[^frogs] The spectral bat, with wings about a metre across, the largest bat in the Americas, eats birds, rodents and other bats.

blocks.caption: Eight bats to sort by what they eat, from a description of the face, teeth or feet. The clue is a description, not a photograph.

items.name: Little brown bat
items.clue: Small, with big ears and a plain snout; rows of tiny pointed teeth.
items.why: Sharp little teeth for cracking insects and big ears for faint echoes: the usual insect-eater's kit.

items.name: Lesser long-nosed bat
items.clue: A long, slender snout and a tongue that reaches far out, ending in a brush; small, weak teeth.
items.why: A long snout and a brush-tipped tongue reach into deep flowers for nectar; it hardly needs teeth.

items.name: Common vampire bat
items.clue: Two razor-edged upper front teeth, very few cheek teeth, and small pits around the nose.
items.why: Blade-like incisors cut the skin, the heat-sensing pits find warm blood, and there is nothing to chew.

items.name: Greater bulldog bat
items.clue: Huge feet on long legs, each toe with a long, curved, hooked claw; drooping lips.
items.why: Long legs and hooked claws gaff fish from the water's surface.

items.name: Jamaican fruit bat
items.clue: A short, broad face, a deep jaw, and wide flat-topped cheek teeth.
items.why: Wide grinding teeth and strong jaws crush fruit pulp.

items.name: Hoary bat
items.clue: Narrow pointed wings for fast flight in the open, short rounded ears, many small sharp teeth.
items.why: A fast open-air hunter of moths, with an insect-eater's teeth.

items.name: Spectral bat
items.clue: Wings a metre across, a large nose leaf, and long strong canines and slicing cheek teeth.
items.why: The biggest bat in the Americas, with a meat-eater's canines and slicing teeth, eats birds and rodents.

items.name: Egyptian fruit bat
items.clue: Large eyes, a face like a small dog's, no nose leaf, and broad grinding cheek teeth.
items.why: Big eyes for finding its way by sight, and grinding teeth for figs and other fruit.

blocks.text: Every spring, pregnant lesser long-nosed bats, *Leptonycteris yerbabuenae*, fly north from central and southern Mexico into the Sonoran Desert, some as far as southern Arizona, following the flowering of the giant cacti. In late summer they move into the mountain grasslands of southeastern Arizona, where the wild agaves bloom. An agave lives for years as a rosette of thick, spiked leaves, then puts all it has into one flowering stalk, sometimes taller than a house, and dies. The flowers at the top open in the evening, pale and sturdy, with a musty smell, and pour out nectar through the night.

The bat hovers, pushes its head into a cluster of flowers and laps, and comes away with its face and shoulders dusted with pollen. It visits many flowers on many plants in a night and may fly tens of kilometres between roost and feeding grounds. A plant that sets seed only once in its life needs pollen from a different plant, and a bat brings pollen from far away.[^outcross]

Here is the hard question. Hummingbirds drink nectar too, in the same deserts, and they are much smaller, so a flower could feed one more cheaply. Why should an agave open at night, make enough nectar to fuel a 25-gram bat, and shut out hummingbirds? Work out an answer before reading on.

Part of the answer is that a hummingbird cannot do the night shift. It needs light to see and lets its body cool into torpor through the night. That only moves the question: why flower at night at all? Two reasons stand out. In a hot desert, nectar made during the day evaporates and costs water the plant can barely spare; at night the air is cool and the nectar stays put. And the bat is the better courier. Hummingbirds defend small territories, chasing others from the flowers nearby, so pollen they carry moves between neighbouring plants, often close relatives. A bat's furry face holds far more pollen than a beak, and it carries it kilometres. For a plant with one chance to set seed, a large courier that travels far is worth a large meal. Day visitors such as bees and birds do also feed at agave flowers that stay open into the morning, but the flower is built for the night.

Tequila is distilled from one agave, the blue agave of Jalisco. Growers do not let it flower: they cut out the young stalk so that the sugar stays in the heart of the plant, which they roast and ferment, and they plant new fields from the clones that sprout around the base of old plants. Fields of genetically identical agaves are rarely pollinated by bats now, and are more open to disease, since what kills one plant can kill them all. Since 2016 a few distillers have sold "bat friendly" tequila, made by growers who let a small share of their plants flower for the bats.[^tequila]

In the tropics of the Americas, small fruit-eating bats such as the short-tailed fruit bats eat fruits full of tiny seeds: wild peppers, figs, nightshades, the trumpet tree *Cecropia*. A meal passes through a bat in as little as twenty minutes. The bat does not land to drop it. The seeds fall wherever the bat happens to be flying, much of the time over open ground between patches of forest.

Birds eat many of the same fruits, but a bird crosses open pasture only briefly, flies from tree to tree, and drops seeds where it perches. So when forest is cleared for pasture and then left, birds seed its edges and the ground under any lone tree, and the bats seed the middle. The plants that grow from those small seeds are **pioneers**, quick-growing plants that need open sun, and they shade out the grass, attract more animals and make room for forest trees. In Chiapas, in southern Mexico, Rodrigo Medellín and Osiris Gaona found in the 1990s that bats were carrying more seeds than birds into disturbed land.

blocks.caption: A strip of pasture 300 metres wide beside a forest, left alone after clearing, with seeds arriving each year from birds and from fruit bats. Play the years with and without the bats, and try leaving one tree standing. An illustrative model.
blocks.task: Play twenty years with the bats, then without them

blocks.text: Fruit bats of the Old World, the flying foxes and their kin, do the same with bigger seeds and over longer distances, and on islands of the Pacific a single species of flying fox may be the only animal left that can carry a large seed from one valley to the next. When it is hunted out, those trees stop spreading.

blocks.caption: Five questions on what bats eat
blocks.task: Choose the best answer to each

items.ask: Why does a gift of a few grams of blood cost a full vampire bat only a few hours but give a hungry one most of a day?
choices: A full bat is losing weight fast and a hungry one slowly, so the same weight is fewer hours on one and more on the other
The donor has extra blood stored in its fat, which it can easily spare after a good night of feeding
Hungry bats digest blood twice as efficiently as full ones, so each gram they receive goes much further
items.why: A bat that has just fed sheds water and weight quickly; one near starvation loses weight slowly. The same grams cover few hours near the top of the curve and many near the bottom.

items.ask: In a vampire roost where some bats take blood but never give, which sharing rule leaves those cheats worst off?
choices: Give only to bats that have fed you before
Give to any hungry roost-mate who asks
Give only to your own relatives
items.why: A cheat never feeds anyone, so under a rule of paying back no one owes it a meal. Giving to everyone, or to family, feeds cheats along with everyone else.

items.ask: A vampire bat that fails to feed one night in fourteen, with no help, is most likely to die how?
choices: By failing two nights in a row at some point, since it starves about 60 hours after a meal
By slowly losing condition over months of slightly too little blood each night
By eating too much on the nights it does feed and being unable to fly
items.why: Two failures in a row are rare on any one night but likely over a year. Without sharing, most adults would be dead within a year.

items.ask: Why does a wild agave in the desert flower at night and feed bats rather than hummingbirds?
choices: Night nectar loses less water, and a bat carries more pollen much further, to unrelated plants
Hummingbirds cannot reach the nectar of agave flowers because they hover too high above them
Bats need less nectar than hummingbirds, because they are cooler and spend the day asleep
items.why: Cool nights save the plant's water, and a bat with a pollen-dusted face visits plants far apart, while a hummingbird defends a few flowers close together.

items.ask: A cleared pasture is left alone next to a tropical forest. Which animals are most likely to start plants growing in its middle, far from any tree?
choices: Fruit bats, which drop small seeds in flight over open ground
Fruit-eating birds, which drop seeds mostly while perched in trees
Insect-eating bats, which carry seeds stuck to their fur
items.why: Birds seldom linger over open ground and mostly drop seeds where they perch. Fruit bats pass seeds within minutes of eating, wherever they are flying.

trpv1.title: One gene, two proteins
trpv1.text: Cells can cut the message copied from a gene in more than one way, a process called splicing, and so make different proteins from the same gene. In the vampire's heat-sensing nerve cells most of the TRPV1 made is a shorter form, which opens at a lower temperature than the full-length form the bat's other nerve cells make.

draculin.title: Medicine from spit
draculin.text: Vampire saliva holds several substances that keep blood flowing. One, a clot-dissolving enzyme later named desmoteplase, was tested as a treatment for strokes, though it failed to beat existing drugs in large trials.

carter.title: Raising the stakes
carter.text: Grooming costs little and is easy to stop if a partner does not groom back, so building up from grooming to blood lets two bats test each other before either risks a meal. Biologists call this raising the stakes.

frogs.title: Calling for a mate, and dinner
frogs.text: Male túngara frogs make a whine followed by chucks. Females prefer calls with more chucks, but so do fringe-lipped bats, which find those calls easier to locate. So the frogs that attract the most mates also attract the most bats.

outcross.title: Why pollen from far away
outcross.text: Seeds from a plant fertilised by its own pollen, or by a close relative's, often grow weaker, because harmful versions of genes are more likely to be paired up. Pollen from a distant plant is less likely to be related.

tequila.title: Bats back off the list
tequila.text: The lesser long-nosed bat was listed as endangered in the United States in 1988 and in Mexico soon after. As its roosts were protected and its numbers recovered, the United States took it off the list in 2018, the first bat to be removed for recovery.
